claims.text: What the strip looks like RBBB plus left axis deviation (RBBB + LAFB) or RBBB plus right axis deviation (RBBB + LPFB).
claims.quote: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) with left anterior fascicular block (LAFB), manifested as left axis deviation (LAD) RBBB and left posterior fascicular block (LPFB), manifested as right axis deviation (RAD) in the absence of other causes

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) QRS: RBBB pattern
claims.quote: The ECG will show typical features of RBBB plus either left or right axis deviation.

claims.text: Axis: left with LAFB; right with LPFB (once other causes of RAD are excluded)
claims.quote: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) with left anterior fascicular block (LAFB), manifested as left axis deviation (LAD) RBBB and left posterior fascicular block (LPFB), manifested as right axis deviation (RAD) in the absence of other causes

claims.text: RBBB + LAFB is the more common of the two
claims.quote: RBBB + LAFB is the most common of the two patterns.

claims.text: “Trifascicular block” as commonly used: bifascicular block + first-degree AV block — an imprecise historical term
claims.quote: Trifascicular block: Bifascicular block + first-degree AV block (historical term; imprecise but still used).

claims.text: True trifascicular block: bifascicular block + third-degree AV block
claims.quote: True trifascicular block refers to the presence of conduction delay in all three fascicles below the AV node (RBBB, LAFB, LPFB), manifesting as bifascicular block and 3rd degree AV block.

claims.text: Warning signs of impending trifascicular block: alternating LBBB/RBBB, or RBBB with alternating fascicular blocks
claims.quote: Normal sinus rhythm with alternating LBBB/RBBB RBBB with alternating fascicular blocks on a beat-to-beat basis

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: two of the three fascicles are blocked, so the ventricles are activated through the one that remains
claims.quote: Bifascicular block involves conduction delay below the atrioventricular node in two of the three fascicles: Conduction to the ventricles is via the single remaining fascicle

claims.text: Ischemic heart disease (40–60%), structural heart disease (50–80%), aortic stenosis, anterior MI, Lenègre-Lev disease, congenital heart disease, hyperkalemia (resolves with treatment)
claims.quote: Ischaemic heart disease (40-60% cases) Structural heart disease (50-80% association) Aortic stenosis Anterior MI (occurs in 5-7% of acute AMI) Lenègre-Lev disease Congenital heart disease Hyperkalaemia (resolves with treatment)

claims.text: New bifascicular block with chest pain is highly associated with proximal LAD occlusion, even without ST changes
claims.quote: A new-onset bifascicular block in the context of chest pain is highly associated with proximal LAD occlusion, even in the absence of ST-segment changes.

claims.text: Symptoms Progression to complete heart block is 1–4% per year overall, about 1% when symptom-free, and 17% a year in patients presenting with syncope
claims.quote: Overall rate of progression to complete heart block is 1-4% per year In symptom free patients, these figures are ~1% per year Patients presenting with syncope have a 17% annual risk of progression

claims.text: Treatment Bifascicular block needs no direct treatment unless intermittent second- or third-degree AV block is present
claims.quote: Bifascicular blocks require no direct treatment unless intermittent second- or third-degree AV block is present.

claims.text: Syncope or presyncope: admit and monitor; pacemaker if no other cause is found
claims.quote: Syncope or presyncope in the context of a bifascicular block is an indication for admission and monitoring. If other causes of syncope are not identified on work-up, pacemaker insertion is recommended

claims.text: True trifascicular block (with third-degree AV block) requires a pacemaker
claims.quote: Patients with true trifascicular block (associated third degree AV block) will require pacemaker insertion

claims.text: Asymptomatic bifascicular block with first-degree AV block is not an indication for pacing
claims.quote: Asymptomatic bifascicular block with first degree AV block is not an indication for pacing (class III)
